definition: Soviet moral-legal category meaning 'social parasitism' — living without socially useful labor — deployed against those whose lifestyles (including sex workers and homosexuals) were deemed incompatible with socialist norms.
notes: Primarily a work-ethics and ideological term, not intrinsically sexual; included in sexuality indices because it was used to prosecute prostitutes, gay men, and the sexually dissolute under the 1961 anti-parasitism decree. Joseph Brodsky was famously convicted under it. Recognition higher among adults 40+ who lived under the Soviet system.

definition: Sexual licentiousness or moral looseness; a condemnatory compound phrase used in both Soviet official discourse and Orthodox moral teaching to denounce unrestrained sexual behavior.
notes: Распущенность alone means 'lack of discipline/moral looseness'; the compound specifies the sexual domain. Stilted and formal — never street slang. Heard in official speeches, church homilies, and moralizing journalism.

definition: Free love; the early-Soviet revolutionary ideology, most associated with Alexandra Kollontai, that rejected bourgeois marriage as a property institution and advocated sexual relationships based on desire and mutual consent alone.
notes: Prominent in 1917–1930 Bolshevik sexual politics before Stalin reversed course in the 1930s and reimposed conservative family norms. Now used historically, ironically, or in leftist discourse. Mapped to ethical_non_monogamy as closest concept, though free love carries an explicit anti-institutional ideological charge absent from ENM.

definition: Bourgeois morality; Marxist-Leninist shorthand for the sexual and family ethics of the capitalist class — monogamy, premarital chastity, property-based marriage — condemned in Soviet thought as ideological tools of class oppression.
notes: Ironic historical arc: early Soviets condemned bourgeois sexual conservatism, yet by the 1930s Soviet society became more sexually conservative than what it mocked. Still heard in contemporary leftist or satirical discourse. Recognition skews older.

definition: Decadentism; Soviet critical term for the perceived cultural and moral degeneration of bourgeois society, encompassing sexual permissiveness, aesthetic excess, nihilism, and despair.
notes: Derived from упадок (decline/decay). In Soviet literary criticism it targeted Symbolist and Decadent artists; in moral discourse it condemned Western sexual and cultural excess as evidence of capitalist collapse. Very low recognition among speakers under 40.

definition: Fornication or sexual immorality; in Orthodox Christian theology one of the eight capital passions, encompassing all non-marital sexual acts and regarded as a sin against God and the body.
notes: Church Slavonic root word from which блудница (harlot), блудный (prodigal/lecherous), and распутство derive. Distinct from прелюбодеяние (adultery specifically). Carries both theological weight and mild everyday crudeness — used colloquially to mean 'lechery' without religious framing.

definition: Adultery; in Orthodox theology and pre-revolutionary Russian law, sexual intercourse by a married person with someone other than their spouse — a more specific and more severely condemned sin than блуд.
notes: Strictly means adultery (violation of marital fidelity); the registry's 'fornication' concept covers pre-marital sex and is not exact. In Orthodox confession, прелюбодеяние and блуд are enumerated as distinct sins. Formal, ecclesiastical register — never colloquial.

definition: The sin of fornication or lust; a set phrase from Orthodox moral theology naming sexual immorality as a sin against both God and the temple of the body.
notes: Compound phrase: блудный (lecherous/fornicating — same root as 'prodigal' in блудный сын, the Prodigal Son) + грех (sin). Common in Orthodox confessional and homiletic contexts. Slightly higher crude score than блуд alone due to the explicit 'sin' framing intensifying the moral charge.

definition: Sinful; adjective applied in Orthodox and broader Russian cultural discourse to characterize sexual desires, thoughts, or acts as contrary to divine law and spiritually corrupting.
notes: General religious adjective. Applied to sexuality to frame desire as inherently morally suspect — e.g., греховные мысли (sinful thoughts), греховные желания (sinful desires). Widely used outside strictly religious contexts in everyday moralizing speech.

definition: Sin; in sexual contexts, the Orthodox and broader Russian cultural framing of sexual desire and non-marital sex as a transgression against divine law — the foundational moral category governing all sexuality in religious discourse.
notes: Extremely high-frequency word with many non-sexual applications. Sexual meaning is the dominant application in Orthodox moral theology, activated by collocations: грехи плоти (sins of the flesh), введение в грех (leading into sin). Mapped to carnal_desire as the closest available registry concept.

definition: Ritual and moral impurity; in Orthodox theology, a state of spiritual uncleanness caused by sexual acts, menstruation, nocturnal emission, or other bodily events, requiring prayer and abstinence before full participation in worship.
notes: Encompasses both ritual impurity (temporary, cleansable through prayer) and moral impurity (sinful). Has strong Hebrew Bible antecedents (טָמֵא / tāmēʾ) transmitted through the Septuagint. Broader and more theologically precise than the registry's 'indecency,' which implies public-decency violation rather than ritual uncleanness.

definition: Chastity or sexual purity; in Orthodox Christianity, a cardinal virtue encompassing pre-marital virginity, marital fidelity, and the disciplined subordination of sexual desire to spiritual order.
notes: Etymology: целый (whole/intact) + мудрость (wisdom) — 'wholeness of mind.' Broader than mere abstinence: it is an attitude of integrated purity governing the whole person. Highly esteemed in Orthodox monastic and lay ascetic tradition. Closer to the Latin 'castitas' than to simple virginity.

definition: Carnal sin or sin of the flesh; Orthodox phrase for any sin rooted in bodily appetite, predominantly applied to sexual transgressions.
notes: Плотский derives from плоть (flesh). Nearly interchangeable with блудный грех in common use but technically broader — can include gluttony and other physical sins — though the sexual application is overwhelmingly dominant in confessional and homiletic contexts.

definition: Sodomy; in Russian Orthodox and historical legal usage, anal intercourse or other non-procreative sexual acts, historically criminalized and strongly condemned as a sin against nature and God.
notes: Borrowed from the biblical city of Sodom via Church Slavonic and Latin. Criminalized in Russia under Soviet Article 121 until 1993. Prominently revived in contemporary Russian anti-LGBT rhetoric since 2013; recognition has risen accordingly. Carries both theological condemnation and legal-historical register.

definition: Sodomite; in Orthodox theology and traditional Russian public discourse, a man who practices anal sex — used almost exclusively as a condemnation of homosexual men.
notes: Religious-legal pejorative. Usage has intensified sharply in Russian public discourse since the 2013 'gay propaganda' law, deployed by conservative commentators and clergy as an alternative to gay/homosexual that carries maximum moral-historical condemnation. Crude score reflects its function as a slur.

definition: Harlot or fornicatrix; in Orthodox usage, a woman guilty of sexual immorality — encompassing both prostitutes and promiscuous women who commit блуд.
notes: Feminine form derived from блуд. Famous from the Gospel narrative of the sinful woman (traditionally conflated with Mary Magdalene). Distinct from проститутка (prostitute) by its theological-moral rather than transactional framing. Carries the dual sense of sexual sinner and fallen woman; the condemnation is moral, not merely commercial.

definition: Fallen woman; a 19th-century Russian literary and social euphemism for a woman who has lost her sexual virtue through seduction, coercion, or poverty-driven prostitution, framed as a social tragedy rather than purely moral condemnation.
notes: Peak in Russian realist literature: Dostoevsky's Sonya Marmeladova, Tolstoy's Katyusha Maslova. The 'fall' (падение) implies a descent from social respectability. Carries more pathos and class-critical nuance than блудница, which is purely condemnatory. The term shaped 19th-century reform movements around rescuing такие женщины.

definition: Repentance or penance; in Orthodox Christianity, the sacramental and psychological process of confessing, regretting, and committing to turn away from sexual sin — the prescribed institutional response to блуд and плотский грех.
notes: Not inherently sexual but central to Orthodox sexual ethics as the culturally enforced mechanism for processing and renouncing sexual transgression. Mapped to sexual_repression because the institutional requirement of покаяние is a primary vehicle through which Russian religious culture internalizes guilt about sexuality. Distinct from Catholic penance: Orthodox покаяние emphasizes inner transformation over prescribed acts.

definition: Spiritual delusion (prelest); in Orthodox ascetic theology, a dangerous state of self-deception where a person believes demonic or carnal temptations — including sexual ones — to be divinely inspired, leading to spiritual pride and destruction.
notes: CRITICAL DISAMBIGUATION: The common modern Russian word прелесть means 'charm/beauty/delight' (recognition ~99%) — this is an entirely different, unrelated sense. The Orthodox theological meaning documented here is known primarily by monastics, theologians, and the Orthodox educated (~28%). In ascetic texts, sexual temptation is a primary gateway into прелесть. The English transliteration 'prelest' exists in Orthodox theological writing but has no common secular equivalent. Proposed slug: orthodox_spiritual_delusion.

definition: Temptation; in sexual contexts, the experience of being drawn toward sexual sin — understood in Orthodox theology as a trial of the soul and an opportunity to choose virtue or fall into блуд.
notes: Extremely common word with many non-sexual applications (temptation to steal, to lie, etc.). Sexual temptation is the most culturally prominent application in Orthodox and general Russian religious discourse. Mapped to lust as the closest registry concept for the sexual valence, though искушение denotes the external allure more than the internal craving.

definition: Sweetness of sin; a theological phrase acknowledging the seductive pleasure of sexual transgression, used in Orthodox homiletics to explain why believers succumb and to underscore the mortal danger of carnal desire.
notes: Phrase from Orthodox homiletic and confessional literature. Notable for its phenomenological honesty: the сладость (sweetness/pleasure) is acknowledged as real, not dismissed, making the warning more sophisticated — the pleasure is the trap. Found in patristic texts translated into Church Slavonic and in 19th-century Russian religious writers.

definition: Flesh; in Orthodox and biblical usage, the corporeal nature of the human being with its appetites and passions — especially sexual desire — understood as the domain of carnal temptation opposed to the spirit.
notes: Church Slavonic word distinct from the neutral тело (body). The biblical antithesis плоть vs. дух (flesh vs. spirit) is foundational to Orthodox sexual ethics. Key collocations: грехи плоти (sins of the flesh), похоти плоти (lusts of the flesh), умерщвление плоти (mortification of the flesh). Not crude in itself — its gravity is theological.

definition: Mortification of the flesh; the Orthodox and broader Christian ascetic practice of deliberately suppressing bodily appetites — through fasting, cold exposure, sleep deprivation, and physical austerities — as a discipline against sexual desire and carnal passion.
notes: Умерщвление = 'killing off/deadening.' Goes well beyond sexual abstinence to include active physical self-punishment. Central to Orthodox monasticism and advocated in patristic ascetic literature (Evagrius, John Climacus). Mapped to sexual_abstinence as closest registry concept, though the practice is markedly more physically demanding and involves deliberate bodily suffering rather than mere restraint.

definition: Lustful or lascivious; an archaic adjective, influenced by Church Slavonic, applied to people, thoughts, or glances characterized by intense carnal sexual appetite.
notes: Archaic form; the modern equivalent is похотливый (same meaning, fully current). Derived from похоть (lust/carnal desire). Found primarily in religious texts, 18th–19th century literature, and deliberately archaizing registers. Recognition among speakers under 35 is low; older speakers recognize it readily from religious or literary exposure.

definition: Shameless; applied in Orthodox moral discourse and everyday Russian speech to someone — especially a woman — who displays sexual behavior without remorse, guilt, or social concealment, violating the shame-based norms that regulate sexuality.
notes: Literally без (without) + стыд (shame) → бесстыжий. Shame (стыд) functions as the primary internal regulator of sexual behavior in Russian honor-shame culture; бесстыжий names its absence. Applied with particular severity to women who display sexuality publicly or without apparent guilt. Still actively used in colloquial Russian — not archaic. The 'approximate' translation quality reflects that 'shameless' in English has largely lost its specifically sexual sting.
